title: Plancherel transform of an L2 weak partial derivative
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field]. Let $m\geq1$ be an integer, equip $\mathbf R^m$ with its Euclidean norm and Lebesgue measure, and write $L^2(\mathbf R^m;\mathbf C)$ for measurable square-integrable complex functions modulo almost-everywhere equality. For $f\in L^2$, let $\widehat f\in L^2$ denote the Plancherel Fourier transform, the continuous extension from Schwartz functions of $f\mapsto(\xi\mapsto\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx)$; Schwartz functions are smooth functions whose derivatives decrease faster than every inverse polynomial. Fix a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbf N^m$, put $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$, $\partial^\alpha=\prod_i\partial_{x_i}^{\alpha_i}$ and $\xi^\alpha=\prod_i\xi_i^{\alpha_i}$. Let $u,v\in L^2$ satisfy $$\int_{\mathbf R^m}v(x)\phi(x)\,dx=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbf R^m}u(x)\partial^\alpha\phi(x)\,dx$$ for every smooth compactly supported complex function $\phi$. Then any measurable representatives $h$ of $\widehat u$ and $k$ of $\widehat v$ satisfy $$k(\xi)=(2\pi i)^{|\alpha|}\xi^\alpha h(\xi)\quad\text{for almost every }\xi.$$ In particular $\xi\mapsto\xi^\alpha h(\xi)$ is square-integrable.

proof.text: Put $n=|\alpha|$ and $c=2\pi i$, and choose measurable representatives $u_0,v_0$ of $u,v$. The weak identity extends to every Schwartz test $\theta$. Indeed, apply [lem-sfb-schwartz-cutoff-l2-approximation] with $s=n$ to get compact smooth $\theta_N$ with $\theta_N\to\theta$ and $\partial^\alpha\theta_N\to\partial^\alpha\theta$ in $L^2$. All these functions are square-integrable by that assertion and [lem-sfb-schwartz-l2-coordinate-calculus]. By [lem-sfb-l2-product-integral-bound], the two errors in the weak identity are bounded by $\|v_0\|_2\|\theta_N-\theta\|_2$ and $\|u_0\|_2\|\partial^\alpha\theta_N-\partial^\alpha\theta\|_2$, respectively, and tend to zero. Passing to the limit gives $\int v_0\theta=(-1)^n\int u_0\partial^\alpha\theta$.

proof.text: For every Schwartz $\psi$, repeated coordinate multiplication and differentiation preserve the Schwartz class by [lem-sfb-schwartz-l2-coordinate-calculus]. Iterating the first-order rule of [lem-sfb-schwartz-fourier-coordinate-rule] gives $\partial^\alpha\mathcal F\psi=\mathcal F(q_\alpha\psi)$, where $q_\alpha(\xi)=(-c)^n\xi^\alpha$. Explicitly start with $\beta=0$, where the formula is the identity; if it holds for an ordered list of coordinate derivatives with multiplier $q_\beta$, applying $\partial_{x_j}$ gives $\mathcal F(-c\xi_jq_\beta\psi)$. Append the $\alpha_j$ copies of each coordinate in the order defining $\partial^\alpha$. The final multiplier is $(-c)^n\prod_j\xi_j^{\alpha_j}$, and every intermediate multiplier times $\psi$ is Schwartz. No lower derivative of $u$ is used.

proof.text: We need the forward bilinear test identity. Let $a\in L^2$, let $b$ be a measurable representative of $\mathcal F_2a$, and let $a_0$ represent $a$. By [lem-sfb-l2-inverse-fourier-test-duality], $\mathcal G_2\mathcal F_2a=a$ and, evaluated on the Schwartz test $\mathcal F\psi$, $\int(\mathcal F\psi)a_0=\int\mathcal G(\mathcal F\psi)b=\int\psi b$. The last equality is the Schwartz inverse law of [lem-sfb-schwartz-fourier-coordinate-rule]. Thus $\int b\psi=\int a_0\mathcal F\psi$. All pairings here are integrable by [lem-sfb-schwartz-l2-coordinate-calculus] and [lem-sfb-l2-product-integral-bound]. This identity applies to the chosen representatives by its statement.

proof.text: Apply step 3 first to $(a,b)=(v,k)$ and then to $(u,h)$ with test $q_\alpha\psi$. Step 1 is applicable to $\theta=\mathcal F\psi$ since this is Schwartz by [lem-sfb-schwartz-fourier-coordinate-rule]. Step 2 identifies its derivative. Consequently, for every Schwartz $\psi$, $$\int k\psi=\int v_0\mathcal F\psi=(-1)^n\int u_0\mathcal F(q_\alpha\psi)=(-1)^n\int hq_\alpha\psi=\int c^n\xi^\alpha h\psi.$$ The last sign is $(-1)^n(-c)^n=c^n$. These are bilinear pairings throughout, so no conjugation or reflected frequency is introduced.

proof.text: Let $w(\xi)=k(\xi)-c^n\xi^\alpha h(\xi)$. By [lem-sfb-lp-local-integrability] at $p=2$, both $h$ and $k$ are locally integrable. Hence $w$ is locally integrable: on a sufficiently small bounded neighborhood where $h,k$ have finite absolute integrals, the polynomial $c^n\xi^\alpha$ is bounded, and $\int|w|\leq\int|k|+\sup|c^n\xi^\alpha|\int|h|<\infty$. It is measurable since $h,k$ are. Every compactly supported smooth real $g$, regarded as complex, is Schwartz by [lem-sfb-schwartz-test-inclusion-integrability]. Step 4 gives $\int gw=0$; the two terms are integrable since $g$ and $\xi^\alpha g$ are Schwartz by [lem-sfb-schwartz-l2-coordinate-calculus], and the L2 product bound applies. Use [lem-sfb-smooth-test-ae-separation] with the open set $U=\mathbf R^m$ to conclude $w=0$ almost everywhere, exactly the required identity.

proof.text: Since $c\ne0$, the established identity gives $\xi^\alpha h=c^{-n}k$ almost everywhere. Thus $\int|\xi^\alpha h|^2=|c|^{-2n}\int|k|^2<\infty$, including $n=0$. The argument began with arbitrary measurable representatives $h,k$, so it proves the representative-independent assertion as stated.
